stem: Name one visible difference between Map A and Map B.
answer: A shows water features; B shows country borders.
steps: Names a visible detail on each map.
samples: A names a river; B names countries. | Both show every detail.

stem: Circle the four map parts on Trail Map.
answer: Title, legend, north arrow and scale bar circled.
steps: All four parts found; ungraded retrieval.
samples: Title, legend, arrow and bar circled. | Only the title circled.

stem: What does Trail Map’s dotted line mean?
answer: Walking trail.
steps: Uses the printed legend; ungraded retrieval.
samples: Walking trail. | River.

stem: The route uses 4 whole bars. Each bar represents 50 meters. How far is it?
answer: 200 meters, because 4 times 50 is 200.
steps: Counts four represented lengths; ungraded retrieval.
samples: 200 meters. | 4 meters.

stem: On Trail Map, which direction is page-up?
answer: East: north points left, so east points up.
steps: Uses the arrow rather than the page edge; ungraded retrieval.
samples: East. | North.

stem: Match the map-parts question to its information strip.
answer: How do map parts help us locate features? matches Map parts.
steps: Recall: a supporting question helps answer the big question. | Read the supplied question. | Match it to the Map parts strip.
samples: How do map parts help us locate features? matches Map parts. | Which pencil is prettiest?

stem: Sort the strips into needed information and unrelated information.
answer: Needed: map parts, distance, scale, boundaries, grid. Unrelated: pencil.
steps: Five map-information strips together; pencil strip apart.
samples: Map parts helps; pencil does not. | Pencil helps locate features.

stem: Annotate one useful detail on Map A or Map B.
answer: One visible detail annotated with a defensible use.
steps: Points to a printed feature or border. | Names what that detail helps a reader find.
samples: The river line helps trace water. | It is my favorite.

stem: Why might the two readers ask different map questions?
answer: The student needs a walking route. The traveler needs country locations to compare countries. Their different purposes call for different map details.
steps: Explains how the two stated purposes lead to different needed map information. Accept another supported comparison.
samples: Walking to school needs local paths; comparing countries needs country locations. | Both readers need the same details because I like them.

practice: Exit box; independent paper; judged after class
stem: Explain why the answer matters to both readers.
answer: Paths help the student find a walking route. Country locations help the traveler compare countries.
steps: Explains a defensible need for each reader. | Contrasts the two uses without relying on preference alone.
samples: Paths help the student find a walking route. Country locations help the traveler compare countries. | Only my favorite matters.

stem: The hatch tag says river. Repair the tag using Map A’s key.
answer: Change river to lake.
steps: Matches the hatched enclosed mark to lake, not river.
samples: Lake. | River because it looks long.

stem: A made-up map’s north arrow points down. Repair the claim: page-up is north.
answer: Page-up is south.
steps: Orients from the arrow; does not change a real geographic map arrow.
samples: Page-up is south. | Page-up stays north.

stem: Trace Mississippi River on Map A.
answer: Follows the solid line through the central land area.
steps: Traces the named river line, not a leader or coast.
samples: The central solid river line traced. | Coast traced.

stem: Trace Lake Superior’s enclosed outline on Map A.
answer: The hatched enclosed Lake Superior outline traced.
steps: Finds the leader endpoint and traces the enclosed water feature.
samples: Enclosed hatched lake traced. | River line traced.

stem: Point to Pacific Ocean on Map A.
answer: The water west of the continent.
steps: Locates the named ocean; no location pair or category explanation.
samples: Water west of the continent. | Interior land.

stem: Write one observation using Map A’s key.
answer: The solid line marks a river; the hatch marks a lake. Accept one accurate observation.
steps: Names a key mark and its meaning.
samples: The hatch marks a lake. | Long shapes are always rivers.

stem: A triangle tag says water. Its new key says high land. Repair the tag.
answer: Change water to high land.
steps: Uses the supplied fresh key; independent of the exit symbols.
samples: High land. | Water.

practice: Exit box; independent paper; judged after class
stem: Mark Hudson Bay and Lake Winnipeg on Exit Water Map.
answer: Hudson Bay: broad inlet at 1. Lake Winnipeg: enclosed hatched water at 2.
steps: Both features correctly marked on the map.
samples: 1 and 2 correctly marked. | Both marks on 1.

stem: Use its key to explain which feature is a lake.
answer: Lake Winnipeg: its enclosed outline has the diagonal hatch that the key assigns to a lake.
steps: Names Lake Winnipeg. | Links the enclosed hatched mark to the lake key, not just the name.
samples: Lake Winnipeg has the enclosed hatched mark shown for lakes. | The name alone proves it.

stem: A new key assigns dots to hills. Repair the tag: dots mean water.
answer: Dots mean hills.
steps: Follows the supplied fresh key.
samples: Dots mean hills. | Dots mean water.

stem: Trace the Rocky Mountains patch on Map A.
answer: The hatched western mountain patch traced.
steps: Follows the leader to the patterned patch. | Uses a physical grouping, not a country border.
samples: Hatched western patch traced. | Country border traced.

stem: Match the Sonoran Desert patch to its key symbol.
answer: Dotted patch matches desert.
steps: Matches the dotted patch to desert.
samples: Dots match desert. | Hatching matches desert.

stem: A caption says the Navajo Nation existed only long ago. Rewrite it using Source 3N.
answer: The Navajo Nation has lands in Utah, Arizona and New Mexico today.
steps: Uses present tense and a fact stated by the named source.
samples: The Navajo Nation has lands today. | The Navajo Nation disappeared.

stem: Name the two Native nations on the source cards.
answer: Navajo Nation and Cherokee Nation. Inuit are an Indigenous people; Nunavut is a territory.
steps: Names Navajo Nation and Cherokee Nation. | Does not turn Nunavut into a Native nation.
samples: Navajo Nation and Cherokee Nation. | Navajo Nation and Nunavut.

stem: Match each silhouette to mountain range or desert.
answer: Peak chain: mountain range. Dotted patch: desert.
steps: Uses the separately printed silhouette key.
samples: Peaks: mountain range; dots: desert. | Both are water.

practice: Exit box; independent paper; judged after class
stem: Explain why missing nation labels cannot prove that land is empty.
answer: The map selects landform information and omits nation labels. Missing labels cannot establish whether people live there.
steps: Explains selection or omission. | Rejects the inference that no label means no inhabitants.
samples: A map can leave out nation labels even where people live. | No label means nobody lives there.

stem: Mark Sierra Madre Occidental and Mojave Desert on Exit Physical Map.
answer: Sierra Madre Occidental is patch 1 in western Mexico. Mojave Desert is patch 2 farther northwest.
steps: Marks both named landforms using the index and patterns.
samples: Range 1; desert 2. | The white country line marked as the range.

stem: A made-up map labels only hills. Can it establish whether a school is there?
answer: No. The map selected hills; it does not establish whether a school exists.
steps: Distinguishes omitted information from evidence of absence.
samples: No; it labels hills only. | No school label means no school.

stem: Point to the Western Hemisphere on the globe and the map.
answer: The western half of the globe; the flat locator shows longitudes west of the prime meridian.
steps: Identifies the western half; review, not a new coordinate lesson.
samples: Western half indicated. | Only the northern half indicated.

stem: Trace the Rocky Mountains and Andes reminders on separate strips.
answer: R trace in North America; A trace along western South America.
steps: Follows each already printed mountain belt. | Keeps its north-to-south orientation.
samples: Two strips follow R and A. | Both strips laid across the ocean.

stem: Place your strips over their matching mountain belts.
answer: R strip overlays R; A strip overlays A, both on the western side of the land.
steps: Preserves location and shape without inventing a continuous belt across the gap.
samples: Both strips cover their original patches. | A single straight strip joins the continents.

stem: Annotate one difference between the two mountain belts.
answer: The Andes form a longer north-to-south belt on this locator; the Rockies slant southeast. Accept visible shape differences.
steps: Names a difference visible in the mapped paths, not ruler distances.
samples: R slants southeast; A runs along the western side. | Both show all landforms.

practice: Exit box; independent paper; judged after class
stem: Mark the Canadian Shield and Amazon Basin on Exit Hemisphere Map.
answer: Shield: patterned region 1 around the northern inland sea. Basin: dotted region 2 in northern South America.
steps: Both mapped region outlines correctly marked.
samples: Shield 1; Basin 2. | Both marks on South America.

stem: Name the continent containing each region.
answer: Canadian Shield: North America. Amazon Basin: South America.
steps: Names a continent for each region, not a country.
samples: Shield: North America; Basin: South America. | Canada and Brazil.

stem: Each new bar represents 40 meters. How far do 3 bars represent?
answer: 120 meters, from three lots of 40.
steps: Builds three equal paper bars and combines their represented lengths.
samples: 120 meters. | 3 meters.

stem: Match a water-tracing task to Map A or Map B.
answer: Map A shows the river line needed for tracing.
steps: Selects A for its visible water information.
samples: A, because it shows the river. | Only one map can ever help anyone.

stem: For Map A's river line, name one reader's task.
answer: A reader can trace the river's course.
steps: Connects the detail to a task, beyond preference.
samples: Trace where the river runs. | Like the prettiest map.

stem: Circle the broader grouping: country or continent.
answer: Continent.
steps: Distinguishes continent from country; ungraded review.
samples: Continent. | Country.

stem: Check whether the prepared strip agrees with its 336-kilometer label.
answer: Yes. The strip is 12 centimeters, three 4-centimeter bars. Each bar represents 112 kilometers.
steps: Set ruler zero at the prepared strip start. | Check that its length is 12 centimeters. | Compare the 4-centimeter practice bar: three bars fit. | Three lots of 112 make 336 kilometers. | The supplied approximate table pairs a whole bar with 70 miles; its half with 35.
samples: Yes. The strip is 12 centimeters, three 4-centimeter bars. Each bar represents 112 kilometers. | A 336-centimeter strip.

stem: Check whether the prepared strip agrees with its 392-kilometer label.
answer: Yes. The 14-centimeter strip holds three whole bars and a half: 112 + 112 + 112 + 56.
steps: Measures the existing strip from zero. | Verifies the supplied label using three whole bars and a half.
samples: Yes. The 14-centimeter strip holds three whole bars and a half: 112 + 112 + 112 + 56. | A 392-centimeter strip.

stem: Check whether the prepared strip agrees with its 448-kilometer label.
answer: Yes. The 16-centimeter strip holds four bars: four lots of 112 kilometers.
steps: Measures the existing strip. | Checks the supplied ground-distance label against four whole bars.
samples: Yes. The 16-centimeter strip holds four bars: four lots of 112 kilometers. | A 448-centimeter strip.

stem: A strip label says 4 kilometers on paper and 112 centimeters on land. Repair the labels.
answer: 4 centimeters on paper; 112 kilometers on land.
steps: Separates ruler units from represented ground units.
samples: 4 centimeters; 112 kilometers. | Both labels say centimeters.

stem: A half-bar label says 56 centimeters on land. Correct its unit.
answer: 56 kilometers on land.
steps: Keeps the represented amount while repairing its ground unit.
samples: 56 kilometers. | 56 centimeters.

stem: Explain how a prepared strip agrees with its ground-distance label.
answer: Each 4-centimeter bar represents 112 kilometers; the measured strip holds the stated number of bars.
steps: Links a ruler reading, whole or half bars, and the existing label. | Does not construct a new strip.
samples: Each 4-centimeter bar represents 112 kilometers; the measured strip holds the stated number of bars. | The ruler directly measures kilometers.

stem: The bar represents 80 kilometers. What ground distance does the marked segment represent?
answer: 200 kilometers. The segment measures 5 centimeters; the 2-centimeter bar fits two-and-a-half times.
steps: Measures the existing segment from zero. | Uses two whole bars and a half to determine 200 kilometers.
samples: 200 kilometers: two-and-a-half 80-kilometer bars. | 5 kilometers.

stem: Repair this strip's ground unit: 224 centimeters. The strip matches two practice bars.
answer: 224 kilometers. Two practice bars represent 112 + 112 kilometers.
steps: Repairs the supplied unit label; compares already prepared whole-bar strips without constructing a length.
samples: 224 kilometers. Two practice bars represent 112 + 112 kilometers. | 224 centimeters.

stem: Match each pair to whole, half or double bars.
answer: 112 kilometers/about 70 miles: whole; 56/about 35: half; 224/about 140: double.
steps: Matches each separate row to its bar length.
samples: Whole 112/70; half 56/35; double 224/140. | Whole 112/112.

stem: A three-bar row says 336 kilometers and about 336 miles. Repair its miles entry.
answer: About 210 miles: three lots of 70.
steps: Adds represented mile distances rather than copying kilometer digits.
samples: 70 + 70 + 70 = about 210 miles. | About 336 miles.

stem: A four-bar row says 448 kilometers and about 140 miles. Repair its miles entry.
answer: About 280 miles, double the double-bar row.
steps: Doubles both entries of the two-bar row.
samples: 140 + 140 = about 280 miles. | About 140 miles.

stem: Double the two-bar row to fill the missing four-bar row.
answer: 4 bars; 448 kilometers; about 280 miles.
steps: Doubles 224 and 140 separately and labels both units.
samples: 448 kilometers; about 280 miles. | 448 in both columns.

stem: Explain one correction using the table.
answer: For three bars, three lots of 70 give about 210 miles. Accept the four-bar correction.
steps: Explains why the stated table equivalence supports the repaired row.
samples: Four bars double two bars, so double 140 miles. | The numbers should look alike.

stem: The table pairs 60 kilometers with about 40 miles. Find one-and-a-half bars in both units.
answer: 90 kilometers and about 60 miles.
steps: Adds a whole and a half of each table entry. | Labels both resulting ground distances.
samples: 90 kilometers and about 60 miles. | 90 kilometers; about 90 miles.

stem: A two-bar row shows 224 miles and about 140 kilometers. Repair the unit labels.
answer: 224 kilometers; about 140 miles.
steps: Keeps the amounts and restores the supplied table units.
samples: 224 kilometers; about 140 miles. | Both amounts are miles.

stem: Underline one detail in each map supporting the supplied claim.
answer: The hall appears in the town view; the city dot appears in the state view.
steps: Review the supplied claim: the views select different information. | Underline hall and city-dot details in the supplied sentences. | Link those details to the given claim, without generating a usefulness argument.
samples: The hall appears in the town view; the city dot appears in the state view. | The claim needs no detail.

stem: Align the paper windows with their matching boxes.
answer: Small window matches town box; wider window matches state box.
steps: Matches extents around the same city location.
samples: Both windows frame the city dot. | Windows placed outside the mapped area.

stem: Cross out labels that disappear when each wider view replaces the closer view.
answer: Town to state: hall, pond, Ash Road. State to continent: city dot and town window.
steps: Identifies information omitted in each actual wider view; does not infer the features vanished.
samples: Hall and pond disappear from the state view; city dot disappears from the continent view. | Every street remains.

stem: Repair this list into one location sentence: hall, pond.
answer: The hall is east of the pond. Accept another true relationship visible on the town map.
steps: Replaces a feature list with a mapped spatial relationship.
samples: The hall is east of the pond. | Hall, pond.

stem: Annotate one detail missing from the wider view.
answer: Ash Road is absent from the state view. Accept a visible local feature omitted there.
steps: Marks a specific omission only; does not write a comparative usefulness explanation.
samples: Ash Road is absent from the state view. Accept a visible local feature omitted there. | Every map shows everything.

stem: Explain how the Denver maps differ in useful detail.
answer: The city view shows local streets; the Colorado view locates Denver but omits those streets. The continent view locates Colorado and omits city detail.
steps: Compares useful visible detail in at least two named views. | Supports the comparison with information retained and omitted.
samples: The city view shows streets. The Colorado view locates Denver but leaves those streets out. | Every view shows every street.

stem: Circle the road label missing from the wider repair window.
answer: Reed Road.
steps: Uses the fresh town and wider windows; ungraded repair of selection.
samples: Reed Road circled. | Every wider map has every road.

stem: Find one detail contradicting the supplied statement.
answer: The continent view has no road lines, though the town view does.
steps: Points to actual mapped information rather than map size or preference.
samples: The continent view has no road lines. | I prefer the town map.

stem: Annotate what the supplied weather-map choice cannot display.
answer: The town view cannot display both separated weather stations in the state view.
steps: Critiques the supplied choice using its coverage; no new navigation or walk case.
samples: The town window does not reach station B. | A town view covers the whole state.

stem: Mark the detail that disproves the supplied water-inventory claim.
answer: The local pond is drawn on the town view but omitted from the continent view.
steps: Uses actual pond depiction and its omission to challenge the claim.
samples: Pond circled on the town map; no pond at the state window on the continent view. | The continent view includes every pond.

stem: Replace the unsupported statement with one supported map detail.
answer: The town view shows Reed Road. Accept another directly visible detail.
steps: Writes a supported replacement tied to a named view.
samples: The town view shows the pond. | The map shows every person.

stem: Which map best supports this walk? Use mapped features to explain your choice.
answer: The city map supports the invented garden-to-hall walk. Fir Street and the Elliott Bay shoreline locate its route.
steps: Selects the city view. | Explains the choice with visible human and environmental features; no separate limit response.
samples: The city view shows Fir Street beside Elliott Bay for this walk. | I like the continent map.

stem: Circle the detail missing from the wide repair window.
answer: Bench.
steps: Compares the two fresh invented windows; accepts the bench symbol or label.
samples: Bench. | Every view shows the bench.

stem: Check the supplied Ontario index trail.
answer: The trail reaches Ontario in cell C3.
steps: Read the index name. | Move to column C, then row 3. | Match the dot and follow the thin division boundary.
samples: The trail reaches Ontario in cell C3. | The Ontario trail ends in cell C2.

stem: Correct the supplied Yukon category record.
answer: Yukon is a territory within Canada, not a country.
steps: Read the division reference. | Replace country with territory. | Keep Canada as the country.
samples: Yukon is a territory within Canada, not a country. | The division is a separate country.

stem: Repair the British Columbia boundary statement.
answer: British Columbia lies inside Canada. Its thin boundary separates Canadian divisions.
steps: Corrects a supplied boundary statement, separately from classifying divisions.
samples: British Columbia lies inside Canada. Its thin boundary separates Canadian divisions. | The division is a separate country.

stem: Correct the Northwest Territories category record.
answer: Northwest Territories is a territory, not a province.
steps: Uses the division reference separately from the boundary slip.
samples: Northwest Territories is a territory, not a province. | Northwest Territories is a province.

stem: Copy one corrected record for the question board.
answer: British Columbia is within Canada. Accept the corrected Northwest Territories category.
steps: Copies a supported correction; collected and returned day 10.
samples: British Columbia is within Canada. Accept the corrected Northwest Territories category. | I like this map.

stem: Use the indexed inset to explain Prince Edward Island's kind of Canadian division.
answer: Prince Edward Island is a province within Canada, not an independent country.
steps: Uses the reference classification and enclosing Canada locator to explain province status.
samples: It is a province within Canada. | It is an independent country.

stem: Repair this record: A Canadian province is a separate country.
answer: A province is a division within Canada.
steps: Corrects the province/country relation without repeating the day 9 exit case.
samples: A province is a division within Canada. | The division is a separate country.

stem: Check the supplied Jalisco index trail.
answer: The trail reaches Jalisco in main-map cell B3.
steps: Read the name and panel. | Follow column B, row 3. | Trace the division boundary within Mexico.
samples: The trail reaches Jalisco in main-map cell B3. | The Jalisco trail ends in main-map cell C3.

stem: Correct this record: Cuba is a Mexican state.
answer: Cuba is a Caribbean country, not a state in Mexico.
steps: Read the Cuba reference and its separate outline. | Replace Mexican state with Caribbean country.
samples: Cuba is a Caribbean country, not a state in Mexico. | Cuba is a Mexican state.

stem: Circle the wrong step in the supplied Jalisco trail.
answer: Circle C3; replace it with B3.
steps: Uses the main map and index; corrects the supplied route rather than performing a three-place search.
samples: Circle C3; replace it with B3. | Circle B3 instead of the supplied wrong C3 step.

stem: Repair this boundary statement: Jalisco contains all of Mexico.
answer: Mexico contains Jalisco. Jalisco is a Mexican state.
steps: Uses the boundary to reverse the false containment relation.
samples: Mexico contains Jalisco. Jalisco is a Mexican state. | The division is a separate country.

stem: Correct this statement: The Caribbean region is one country.
answer: The Caribbean region includes countries and other territories. Cuba is one country there.
steps: Uses region and country accurately; accepts the grouping explanation without naming additional places.
samples: The Caribbean region includes countries and other territories. Cuba is one country there. | The Caribbean region is one country.

stem: Star your corrected region statement for the question board.
answer: The Caribbean region is not one country. It includes Cuba and other places.
steps: Marks the corrected region statement, rather than writing it a second time. Collect and return day 11.
samples: The Caribbean region is not one country. It includes Cuba and other places. | Cuba contains all of the Caribbean.

stem: Use the exit index to mark Sonora and Barbados on the map.
answer: Sonora: S in northwestern Mexico. Barbados: B in the eastern Caribbean inset.
steps: Marks each indexed location in its own outlined place. | No political-category response is scored.
samples: S within Sonora and B within Barbados. | Either mark outside its indexed place.

stem: Repair this boundary record: A Mexican state lies outside Mexico.
answer: A Mexican state is a division within Mexico.
steps: Uses the state/country distinction in a fresh generic record.
samples: A Mexican state is a division within Mexico. | The division is a separate country.

stem: Underline one detail from each practice map supporting the supplied claim.
answer: Map L places Reed County within State R. Map M places Alder City within Reed County.
steps: Links a different visible detail from each map to the supplied containment claim.
samples: Map L places Reed County within State R. Map M places Alder City within Reed County. | The maps are good because I like them.

stem: Find the reversed arrow in the supplied diagram.
answer: State R → Reed County is reversed. Correct: Reed County → State R.
steps: Read the arrow key: is inside. | Compare Map L. | Reverse only the unsupported arrow.
samples: State R → Reed County is reversed. Correct: Reed County → State R. | State R is inside Reed County.

stem: Repair the other reversed arrow using Map M.
answer: Correct Reed County → Alder City to Alder City → Reed County.
steps: Uses is inside consistently; repairs an arrow rather than generating the exit explanation.
samples: Correct Reed County → Alder City to Alder City → Reed County. | Reed County is inside Alder City.

stem: Underline the government detail. Cross out the unsupported past-only statement.
answer: Underline Cherokee Nation has executive, legislative and judicial branches today. Cross out Cherokee Nation has no government today.
steps: Uses the current government source as evidence. Marks present branches, not an unsupported past-only claim.
samples: Underline Cherokee Nation has executive, legislative and judicial branches today. Cross out Cherokee Nation has no government today. | Cherokee Nation has no government today.

stem: Explain one correction to your partner using the arrow key or source.
answer: The arrow means is inside, so Alder City points toward Reed County. Accept a source-based present-government correction.
steps: Two simultaneous 45-second turns; collected and returned day 12.
samples: The arrow means is inside, so Alder City points toward Reed County. Accept a source-based present-government correction. | The larger place must point inside the smaller one.

stem: Complete the Tucson inset's city-to-continent chain.
answer: Tucson, Pima County, Arizona, United States, North America. Kinds: city, county, state, country, continent.
steps: Completes the nested chain in containment order. | Uses the place kinds consistently; no second explanation required.
samples: Tucson city → Pima County → Arizona state → United States country → North America continent. | Pima County contains Arizona.

practice: Exit box; independent paper; judged after class
stem: Explain whether Card N's nation must be an independent country.
answer: No. Citizen Potawatomi Nation has its own government today within the United States.
steps: Uses the held government card and neutral nation reference. | Explains why present nationhood does not require independent-country status.
samples: No. Citizen Potawatomi Nation has its own government today within the United States. | Every nation must be an independent country.

stem: Repair one record using its reference.
answer: County lies inside the example state. Cherokee Nation governs today and need not be an independent country.
steps: Accept the correction matching the assigned record; never put nation on the containment ladder.
samples: County lies inside the example state. Cherokee Nation governs today and need not be an independent country. | The county contains the state.

stem: Circle both zero lines. Shade cell D2 on the letter grid.
answer: Equator and prime meridian circled; column D, row 2 shaded.
steps: Ungraded retrieval: identifies the two zero lines and letter-number cell. | Record access and retrieval gaps without awarding a score.
samples: Equator and prime meridian circled; column D, row 2 shaded. | Prime meridian is the only zero line.

stem: Read star A: latitude first, then longitude.
answer: 10 degrees north, 70 degrees west.
steps: Follow A horizontally to its latitude label: 10 degrees north. | Follow A vertically to its longitude label: 70 degrees west. | Name latitude first. A is a crossing, not a cell.
samples: 10 degrees north, 70 degrees west. | 70 degrees west, 10 degrees north.

stem: Read stars B and C: latitude first, then longitude.
answer: B: 30 degrees north, 80 degrees west. C: 10 degrees south, 20 degrees east.
steps: Reads the two crossing lines for each existing star; preserves hemisphere and order.
samples: B: 30 degrees north, 80 degrees west. C: 10 degrees south, 20 degrees east. | B: 80 degrees west, 30 degrees north.

stem: Match each measurement description to latitude or longitude.
answer: North or south from equator: latitude. East or west from prime meridian: longitude.
steps: Distinguishes direction a line runs from direction its number measures.
samples: North or south from equator: latitude. East or west from prime meridian: longitude. | Latitude measures from the prime meridian.

stem: Mark X at 40 degrees north, 120 degrees west on Exit Grid.
answer: X at the crossing of the 40N parallel and 120W meridian.
steps: Marks the intersection, not a neighboring cell. | Reads north from equator and west from prime meridian; latitude first.
samples: X at the crossing of the 40N parallel and 120W meridian. | X placed using longitude as latitude.

stem: Correct the assigned reference label.
answer: Order: latitude, longitude. Latitude zero: equator. Longitude zero: prime meridian.
steps: Corrects only the assigned order or zero-line error; no point pair is produced.
samples: Order: latitude, longitude. Latitude zero: equator. Longitude zero: prime meridian. | Latitude begins at prime meridian.

stem: Trace arrows A and B. Name the measurement unchanged along each.
answer: A: latitude unchanged. B: longitude unchanged.
steps: A runs along a parallel. B follows a meridian. No full point coordinates required.
samples: A: latitude unchanged. B: longitude unchanged. | A changes latitude; B changes longitude.

stem: Match latitude and longitude headings to their measurement descriptions.
answer: Latitude: north/south from equator. Longitude: east/west from prime meridian.
steps: Matches two supplied headings to separate correct margin descriptions. | No swapped-heading repair or coordinate pair.
samples: Latitude: north/south from equator. Longitude: east/west from prime meridian. | Horizontal lines are longitude.

stem: Trace the second premarked route. Name the measurement unchanged along it.
answer: Latitude stays unchanged along Route C, which follows the 15 degrees north parallel.
steps: Traces Route C along a parallel. | Names its unchanged measurement without producing a full coordinate pair.
samples: Latitude stays unchanged along Route C, which follows the 15 degrees north parallel. | Measure latitude east/west from prime meridian.

stem: Repair Card 3: Every coordinate number measures ground distance.
answer: Coordinate degrees measure angles, not ground-distance units.
steps: Explains degree labels with the general reference, not a supplied coordinate pair.
samples: Coordinate degrees measure angles, not ground-distance units. | A degree label is a kilometer distance.

stem: Explain one heading match using the reference.
answer: Latitude matches north/south from equator; longitude matches east/west from prime meridian. Accept either justified match.
steps: Links one matched heading to its zero-line reference. | All submit the heading match; six may explain for 45 seconds each.
samples: Latitude matches north/south from equator; longitude matches east/west from prime meridian. Accept either justified match. | The first label is whichever is larger.

stem: Give Y's coordinates on Exit Grid.
answer: 20 degrees north, 90 degrees west.
steps: Reads latitude first with both hemisphere directions. | Scores only the coordinate-reading component.
samples: 20 degrees north, 90 degrees west. | Y: 90 degrees west, 20 degrees north.

stem: Repair the assigned grid reference statement.
answer: Latitude comes first and measures north/south from equator; longitude measures east/west from prime meridian.
steps: Corrects assigned ordering or zero-line statement without reading or plotting an assessment point.
samples: Latitude comes first and measures north/south from equator; longitude measures east/west from prime meridian. | Longitude comes first.

stem: Underline evidence in the supplied paragraph. Circle words linking evidence to its claim.
answer: Evidence: A marks Mississippi River; B bounds Mexico. Link: so their details differ.
steps: Identifies source-linked details and the inference linking them to the given claim.
samples: Evidence: A marks Mississippi River; B bounds Mexico. Link: so their details differ. | Only the titles are evidence.

stem: Mark the mismatched detail in Link Card A.
answer: The country-boundary detail from B cannot establish that A shows water features.
steps: Critiques a supplied claim/detail link without adding evidence or writing a new argument.
samples: The country-boundary detail from B cannot establish that A shows water features. | A and B are nice.

stem: Mark the mismatched detail in Link Card B.
answer: The Lake Superior detail from A cannot establish that B shows country boundaries.
steps: Critiques the second supplied link; no missing-evidence completion.
samples: The Lake Superior detail from A cannot establish that B shows country boundaries. | A marks Mississippi River.

stem: Explain why one marked link fails.

steps: Explains one mismatch using the actual source and detail; no completed usefulness argument.
samples: The named map and the claimed information do not match the supplied detail. Accept either specific mismatch. | It supports it because I wrote it.

stem: Explain how both Park Maps serve different needs, using each map and one limit.

samples: Walking Map shows paths beside the pond. Region Map locates the park beside a town. The views answer different questions; Region Map cannot guide path turns. | They are useful because they have titles.

stem: Label C's numbered features using its index.
answer: 1 b, Mackenzie River; 2 e, Great Slave Lake; 3 d, Arctic Ocean; 4 a, Appalachian Mountains; 5 c, Chihuahuan Desert.
steps: Accept either correct index letters or full names. Score each correctly located physical category separately; the unordered index is a name bank.
samples: 1 b; 2 e; 3 d; 4 a; 5 c. | 4 c, confusing mountain range with desert.

stem: Explain which line is a river using C's key.
answer: The solid line is a river because the key assigns solid lines to rivers.
steps: Links the chosen line to the printed key, rather than appearance alone.
samples: The solid line is a river because the key assigns solid lines to rivers. | The dotted boundary is the river.

stem: Explain which direction P lies from Q using the north arrow.

steps: Gives west and an arrow-based reason; accepts a correctly rotated compass drawing.
samples: West. North points right, so page-up is west. | North, because P is above Q.

stem: Find the ground distance from P to Q in kilometers and approximate miles.
answer: 1200 kilometers; about 750 miles. The measured segment is 3 centimeters; the bar is 2 centimeters.
steps: Measures 3 centimeters. | Uses one-and-a-half 800-kilometer bars. | Adds the supplied 500-mile and 250-mile table entries.
samples: 1200 kilometers; about 750 miles. The measured segment is 3 centimeters; the bar is 2 centimeters. | 3 kilometers.

stem: Complete D's location table for its four indexed places.
answer: a Manitoba: province in Canada; b Oaxaca: state in Mexico; c Jamaica: Caribbean country; d Kansas: state in United States.
steps: Use D and its a-d index to locate each place. | Record each place and its political category. The country and territory supplement is unscored reference only.
samples: a Manitoba province; b Oaxaca state; c Jamaica country; d Kansas state. | Every marked region is an independent country.

stem: Complete the city-to-continent record using the Madison inset.
answer: Madison city; Dane County; Wisconsin state; United States country; North America continent.
steps: Completes the four enclosing-place blanks in their correct order.
samples: Madison city; Dane County; Wisconsin state; United States country; North America continent. | Dane is the country containing Wisconsin.

stem: Mark K at 50 degrees north, 100 degrees west.
answer: K at the 50 degrees north/100 degrees west intersection.

samples: K at the 50 degrees north/100 degrees west intersection. | K marked at 50 degrees north, 90 degrees west.

stem: Explain how Card H identifies a named Native nation today.
answer: Chickasaw Nation has its own government today, including elected officials and a supreme court.
steps: Names Chickasaw Nation and explains its present government evidence from Card H. No separate state or independent-country comparison is required.
samples: Chickasaw Nation has elected officials and a supreme court today, showing its own government. | Chickasaw Nation has no government today.

stem: Describe how E's library, park and lake lie relative to one another.
answer: The library is northwest of the park, and the park is beside Lake Monona. Accept west of the park for the library.
steps: Gives a supported relationship locating the library relative to the park. | Gives a supported relationship locating the park relative to Lake Monona. Accept equivalent mapped relationships and a labeled drawing.
samples: The library is northwest of the park; the park is beside Lake Monona. | Library, park, lake.

stem: Use F and G to place Madison within Wisconsin and North America.
answer: F places Madison in southern Wisconsin; G places Wisconsin in North America.
steps: Uses each wider view for a visible nested location, not just a list.
samples: F places Madison in southern Wisconsin; G places Wisconsin in North America. | Every view shows the same information.

stem: Explain which map supports deliveries across Wisconsin, including one detail it omits.
answer: F shows the whole state; it omits local streets shown on E.
steps: Chooses F for statewide coverage. | Names a supported omission; this is planning, not driving directions.
samples: F shows the whole state; it omits local streets shown on E. | F shows every local street.

stem: Explain what C and D establish for a visitor. Support your claim with both maps and a limit.
answer: The maps locate different features: C locates Mackenzie River and D locates Manitoba. Their keys identify physical and political features. Neither establishes residents' languages.
steps: Score claim, reasoning and supported limit here. | Score distinct source-linked evidence in A4b from the same response, without double counting.
samples: The maps locate different features: C locates Mackenzie River and D locates Manitoba. Their keys identify physical and political features. Neither establishes residents' languages. | Maps show everything about every resident.

stem: Scored from the work you handed in. Write nothing here.
answer: A4a names C and D with a different relevant detail from each, explaining both links to its claim.
steps: Score source-linked evidence and the two links only. Do not award the claim twice.
samples: A4a names C and D with a different relevant detail from each, explaining both links to its claim. | Two titles without a relevant detail from each.

stem: Explain why another reader would need C or D for a different question.
answer: A landform researcher asks where the Chihuahuan Desert lies. C locates it for comparing physical regions. Accept another supported reader, question, map and benefit.
steps: Explains why an answer to a different question matters to another reader. | Links a needed map and its relevant information to that reader's purpose; no personal disclosure.
samples: A landform researcher needs C to locate the Chihuahuan Desert for comparing physical regions. | Only my question matters.

stem: Match your private cue to the comparison that addresses it.
answer: Chooses the comparison for symbols/scale, political terms, grid/extent, or evidence.
steps: Matches an assigned priority gap to a supplied example comparison. | Does not repair the held record before Fresh attempt.

stem: Repair Record A using its key and north arrow.
answer: Dashed line is river. Page-right is west when north points down.
steps: Score only the privately assigned symbol or direction component. Use its new legend or printed arrow. No total.
samples: Dashed line is river. Page-right is west when north points down. | Solid line is river because it looks like water.

stem: Build a strip representing 156 kilometers using this new bar.
answer: 9 centimeters, or one and a half 6-centimeter bars: 104 + 52 = 156 kilometers.
steps: Constructs a 9-centimeter strip at actual size. | Links one whole 104-kilometer bar and its half to 156 kilometers.
samples: 9 centimeters; 104 + 52 = 156 kilometers. | A 1.5-centimeter strip.

stem: Repair Record B using the inset key.
answer: Yucatán is a state within Mexico, not a country containing Mexico.
steps: Corrects political category and containment using the new inset; Saskatchewan is reminder only.
samples: Yucatán is a state within Mexico, not a country containing Mexico. | Mexico lies inside the country Yucatán.

stem: Repair Record C using the government reference.
answer: A Native nation can govern itself today within the United States without being a state or independent country.
steps: Corrects the general nation/country confusion, without inventing a Native nation or asking about a child.
samples: A Native nation can govern itself today within the United States without being a state or independent country. | A Native nation must be a United States state.

stem: Repair Record D using its zero-line diagram.
answer: Latitude measures north/south from equator. Longitude measures east/west from prime meridian.
steps: Repairs the two incorrect headings on the fresh diagram. | Uses the printed zero-line references.
samples: Latitude measures north/south from equator. Longitude measures east/west from prime meridian. | Latitude measures east/west from prime meridian.

stem: Repair Record E using the map windows.
answer: The wider window leaves out the street shown in the close view.
steps: Uses visible omission; a wider area does not require every local detail.
samples: The wider window leaves out the street shown in the close view. | The wider view has every street.

stem: Add the missing map detail to the market claim.
answer: V places stalls beside the well, supporting the claim about water access.
steps: Adds the missing V detail and its link to the given market claim. | Another U detail or an attendance count does not fill the gap.
samples: V places stalls beside the well, supporting the claim about water access. | The market has many visitors because both maps exist.

stem: Mark the part you changed. Name the reference that helped.
answer: Identifies a real correction and its relevant reference; no self-awarded score.
steps: Reflection only, retained in folder; not a second scored record.
samples: Identifies a real correction and its relevant reference; no self-awarded score. | Awards points without describing a change.

stem: A made-up family buys food delivered across a border. Explain why our unit question could matter to them.
answer: Understanding delivery connections helps explain food supply or interruptions.
steps: Gives a use for this family, not only class.
samples: They could understand which delivery brings their food. | The teacher likes maps.

stem: A question asks where a lake lies and how nearby residents use it. Name helpful source kinds with each kind's job.
answer: Map/atlas locates it; article/resident account describes uses. Accept alternatives with distinct relevant jobs.
steps: Location kind and experience/use kind; each job explained.
samples: A map locates it; residents' accounts describe uses. | Use the prettiest pages.

stem: Made-up ferry records: a clerk's 2026 trip table; a rider's 2026 crowding blog. A 1990 visitor guide gives old times. Choose two for current ferry use. Support your choice through makers, kinds, dates, and viewpoints.
answer: Clerk table and rider blog: counts and one experience, both 2026. Guide is historical; neither current record describes all riders.
steps: Complementary records; maker/kind/date/viewpoint reasons.
samples: The current table counts trips; the current rider account describes crowding. | The official table proves everyone is happy.

stem: A made-up school made a travel leaflet for school travelers in 1995. It describes that year's buses. Explain its usefulness for researching school travel then and now.
answer: School advice for school travelers in 1995; current routes need a current source. Date and audience constrain use.
steps: Date and audience used; historical evidence distinguished from current proof.
samples: It shows school advice in 1995, not current routes. | Printed means current.

stem: Made-up sign: This park opened in 1950. It has the friendliest ducks. Explain how you would judge the sign's opening-year claim.
answer: Check 1950 in an independent town opening record. Preference neither proves nor cancels the date.
steps: Relevant verification; preference kept separate.
samples: Check the opening record; friendliest does not prove the year. | Friendly ducks prove the year.

stem: Use the map and separately authored geography card. Compare their information about Lake Chapala's country, including one limit of agreement.
answer: Both locate Lake Chapala in Mexico. Location agreement does not establish water quality or other unmeasured facts.
steps: Mexico compared in independent origins; limit stated.
samples: Both put it in Mexico; neither tests the water. | Both agree, so the water is safe.

stem: What can this project record establish about the community's language use?
answer: The Gabriel Dumont Institute develops Michif resources for Métis language work. This establishes current language work, not every Métis person's speech.
steps: Bounded source-based inference; no universal speech claim.
samples: It documents Michif language work by a Métis institute, not everyone's speech. | Every Métis person speaks Michif.

stem: Canada's prime minister leads a government needing the elected House's confidence. Mexico and the United States have presidents. Each has lawmakers and courts. Explain one government difference involving Canada's confidence requirement.
answer: Canada's prime minister leads a government needing the House's confidence; Mexico and the United States have presidents. Accept another difference the card supports.
steps: One supported difference involving needed House support; office titles alone are incomplete.
samples: Canada has a prime minister needing the House's support; Mexico has a president. | Canada's prime minister is its president.

stem: Use the Winnipeg inset and its key. Explain Winnipeg's position using the river symbols.
answer: City marker beside meeting of Red and Assiniboine rivers.
steps: Uses dot and joining river lines, not climate.
samples: The river lines meet beside Winnipeg's dot. | The map proves it is always warm.

stem: Explain how the recorded work connects Montreal to other places.
answer: The federal record describes cargo loaded at Montreal for transport to another port. Loading puts goods into a shipment connecting places.
steps: Connects the recorded loading to goods moving between places.
samples: Loading cargo at Montreal puts goods into a journey to another port. | Everyone in Montreal loads ships.

stem: Made-up leaflet: Lake Dell has the most fun beach. It is 3 kilometers across. An independent survey map records 2 kilometers. Write a report note separating the preference from the disputed measurement.
answer: Most fun is preference; 3 conflicts with 2. Check measurement date/method/place; neither automatically true.
steps: Separates preference; acknowledges unresolved conflict.
samples: Most fun is preference; the widths disagree, so I must check them. | The leaflet is printed, so 3 is right.

stem: The made-up Moss Town map places its marker inland. A report calls it coastal. Write a speaker note correcting the report with map evidence.
answer: Say inland, citing marker away from coast.
steps: Source-grounded correction for listener.
samples: I will say inland because the marker is away from the coast. | Coastal sounds better.

stem: Made-up tram map: Market and Hill stops. Depot list: three trams. Peer explanation: The route has two stops. Only one tram runs. Repair the explanation's accuracy using these records.
answer: The map supports two stops. The depot lists three trams, but does not say how many run. Replace the operating claim with the listed count or state that the running count is unknown.
steps: Repairs the unsupported operating claim using the inventory's limit.
samples: The depot lists three trams; it does not establish how many run. | Three trams must run because three are listed.

stem: Made-up case: one country specializes in glass jars. Another specializes in metal lids. Jar orders rise. Explain how rising jar orders increase reliance between these producers.
answer: More jar orders require more lids from the other producer. Lid sellers increasingly rely on those jar makers' purchases.
steps: Explains increasing deliveries and purchases in both directions.
samples: Jar makers need more lids; lid sellers need the growing purchases. | Glass jars and metal lids.

stem: Use the made-up trade map. Explain what the oats arrow means for both countries.
answer: Canada exports oats; Mexico imports the same shipment.
steps: Correctly interprets the same arrow as export at origin and import at destination.
samples: Canada exports oats and Mexico imports them. | Mexico exports oats to Canada.

stem: Made-up case: a country buys more imported flour. Bakers get steady supplies. Local millers lose orders. Explain the different effects on bakers and local millers.
answer: Bakers gain reliable inputs; redirected purchases reduce local millers' orders.
steps: Both mechanisms within country.
samples: Bakers keep baking; millers sell less because purchases moved abroad. | Everyone wins.

stem: Made-up case: cheaper imported parts lower repair costs. More customers choose repairs instead of replacement tools. Explain the effects on repair services and replacement-tool sellers.
answer: Repairers gain customers as costs fall; replacement sellers lose purchases through substitution.
steps: Both effects explained through changed purchases.
samples: Repairers gain work; replacement sellers lose orders as customers choose cheaper repairs. | All sellers gain.

stem: Made-up Map P sends clay across a border to potters. Workshop Record R shows more pots sold back across that border. State a tentative reliance claim using one detail from each record.
answer: Potters rely on cross-border material and buyers: P supplies clay, R shows return sales.
steps: Tentative claim; distinct relevant details connected.
samples: Potters rely on trade: P supplies clay, and R shows buyers for more pots. | P and R are nice.

stem: Made-up Map S sends foreign cloth to a tailor. Buyer Record T shows lower clothing prices and fewer rival-shop orders. Write a claim explaining uneven trade effects using both records.
answer: S supplies production; T shows lower buyer prices but rival order losses. Link distinct details to uneven effects.
steps: Unequal-effects argument; relevant S and T details.
samples: S supplies cloth; T shows cheaper clothing but fewer rival orders, so effects differ. | Trade makes everyone rich. S and T.

stem: Made-up article: Canadian books reached Mexico in April. They are the best books. Could a dated shipping record verify the April shipment? Explain using its needed details.
answer: Yes, if the record identifies books shipped to Mexico in April. It cannot verify that they are best.
steps: Connects shipment contents, destination and month to the proposed check.
samples: Yes, if it records books sent to Mexico in April. | Any shipping record proves the books are best.

stem: Explain Halifax's location and cargo connection using A and B.
answer: Halifax: Nova Scotia, Atlantic (A); cargo handling connects goods movements (B). No universal job inference.
steps: Location detail from A; cargo connection from B.
samples: A locates Halifax in Nova Scotia; B shows cargo handling. | Halifax is on the Pacific; everyone works on ships.

stem: Name two source kinds for deciding whether bicycle trade helps everyone.
answer: Order records plus affected buyer/producer accounts; accept complementary relevant kinds.
steps: Two helpful kinds suited to purchases/effects.
samples: Orders and affected-group accounts. | Pretty pictures only.

stem: Choose two among D, E, and F for their differing viewpoints.
answer: D and E give producers and buyers, benefits and costs. F alone omits losses. Alternative pair must acknowledge missing evidence and differing experiences.
steps: Complementary evidence chosen considering views.
samples: D and E show workshop and buyer experiences, including losses. | Only agreeing promotions matter.

stem: Gather one useful detail each from D and E.
answer: D: imported components, order growth or group effects. E: buyer prices or rival assembler losses. Name each.
steps: Two distinct relevant attributed details.
samples: D shows imported tubes; E shows cheaper bicycles. | D and E.

stem: Justify D and E using their makers, formats, and settings.
answer: D: Canadian workshop's made-up 2026 order table. E: United States buyers' made-up 2026 comparison. Same case/date, distinct roles/formats show purchases/effects. Evidence only within invented case.
steps: Origin, format and context for both.
samples: D's workshop table traces orders; E's buyer comparison shows effects in this made-up 2026 case. | Tables are always reliable.

stem: Explain how F's purpose limits its evidence.
answer: Undated seller promotion encourages buying but supplies no evidence that every group benefits.
steps: Connects purpose to missing evidence.
samples: F wants sales but gives no group evidence. | A promotion proves everyone gains.

stem: Classify C's statements as checkable claim or opinion.
answer: Prince Rupert in British Columbia is checkable; nicest city is opinion without agreed measure.
steps: Location distinguished from preference.
samples: Location is checkable; nicest is opinion. | Both are facts because printed.

stem: Check C's location claim against A and B.
answer: Both place Prince Rupert in British Columbia. A uses provincial place-name data; B an independently authored federal port list.
steps: Compares actual province detail in both origins.
samples: A places its dot in British Columbia; B lists its port there too. | A and B have names.

stem: Judge C for locating the city and choosing a favorite.
answer: Location is corroborated. Preference cannot choose everyone's favorite or establish superior living conditions; judge claims separately.
steps: Bounded credibility for two uses.
samples: C's location is supported; its liking cannot choose everyone's favorite. | One opinion makes all of C false.

stem: Give one source-supported strength in the peer explanation.
answer: Cargo moves there is supported by B's port entry.
steps: Supported accurate strength.
samples: B supports the cargo statement. | Good because short.

stem: Repair its order, detail, and accuracy using A and B.
answer: Introduce Halifax/location first; add Nova Scotia and port evidence; replace Pacific with Atlantic; remove everyone-works inference.
steps: Order, missing detail and both accuracy faults repaired.
samples: Begin with Halifax in Nova Scotia on the Atlantic; then B's cargo activity. Remove everyone. | Keep Pacific and everyone unchanged.

stem: Explain how D's growing orders increase reliance, including a late-tube effect.
answer: Canadian assembly needs Mexican tubes and United States wheels; more United States orders need more components. Late tubes can interrupt assembly/delivery as reliance grows.
steps: Specialization, growth and delay mechanism.
samples: More orders need more imported components; late tubes can stop assembly. | Each country makes everything alone.

stem: Complete the effects table using D and E.
answer: Canada: workshop workers gain shifts, rival assemblers lose orders. Mexico: supplying workers gain orders, rival tube makers lose sales. United States: buyers pay less, rival assemblers lose orders. Link each to changed purchases.
steps: One gain/loss within each country; each purchase mechanism explained.
samples: Canada: workshop gains, rival loses orders. Mexico: supplier gains, rival loses. United States: buyers pay less, rival assemblers sell less. | Every person in Canada gains.

stem: Explain the countries' connections using one detail each from D and E.
answer: Bounded argument for shared reliance or unequal effects; D's components/orders and E's buyer/rival effects linked. Score claim/reasoning here once; source support separately E10.
steps: Defensible claim and reasoning; distinct relevant D/E evidence.
samples: D needs imported parts; E shows buyer gains and rival losses, so the chain links groups unevenly. | I like bicycles. D and E.

stem: Your revised report, map, and source log. Scored from the work you handed in. Write nothing here.

Include scoped dated population/language information, offices/functions, city locator, natural resource, landmark, analyzed resource/work relationship and coherent order. Score revised components separately.
steps: Four source kinds; six accurate sourced topics; dated scope; map/resource/landmark; analyzed relationship; organization.
samples: A six-topic folder links findings to sources and explains water supporting agriculture. | Favorite places without source links or coverage.

stem: Present one revised source-linked finding.
answer: One supported revised finding naming its source; thirty teacher-heard 45-second slots in 23 minutes. Listener reply is judged separately from retained work in s02-E8b.
steps: Source-linked finding, supported by a relevant detail.
samples: My finding matches this detail in my source. | Best because I like it.

stem: A made-up exhibit planner explains connections among the three countries. Explain why the unit question could help this planner.

steps: Connects the inquiry answer to the stated planner and readers.
samples: The planner can explain which supplies cross borders in the exhibit. | The teacher likes this topic.

stem: Scored from the work you handed in for E6. Write nothing here.
answer: Only E6's multiple-source support: distinct relevant D/E details linked to claim. Do not score claim/reasoning twice.
steps: Relevant D detail; relevant E detail; both linked to argument.
samples: The component chain and buyer/rival effects both support the argument. | D and E are my sources.

stem: Write a smaller question about the made-up two-town bus diagram.
answer: Any smaller question answerable from the supplied route diagram.
steps: Researchable smaller question about a visible route or stop detail.
samples: Which town does each stop serve? | I like buses.

stem: Label each teaching source by kind.
answer: A map; B atlas; C article; D printed digital page. Accept D as an equipment list on a printed digital page.
steps: All four teaching-source labels; allow kind/format overlap supported by contents.
samples: A map; B atlas; C article; D printed digital page. | All are maps.

stem: Label the equipment notice's maker, date, audience, and format.
answer: Caretakers' office; 2010; caretakers; notice.
steps: Maker is caretakers' office; date is 2010; audience is caretakers; format is posted notice.
samples: Caretakers' office; 2010; caretakers; posted notice. | The title alone makes it useful.

stem: Underline the equipment notice's audience and purpose.
answer: Caretakers; preparing equipment.
steps: Underlines caretakers as audience and preparing equipment as purpose.
samples: Caretakers; preparing equipment. | Everyone everywhere.

stem: Match each already labeled claim to its evidence record.
answer: Chair-count claim matches the inventory, but five conflicts with its six chairs. Delivery-day claim matches receipt; favorite color has no agreed factual test.
steps: Inventory tests and contradicts five chairs; receipt supports Monday; color liking has no agreed factual test.
samples: Inventory: six contradicts five; receipt: Monday matches; color: no agreed test. | A liking verifies five chairs.

stem: Mark which teaching notes copy another maker.
answer: B copies A; C is a separate observer, not a copy of A.
steps: Marks B and traces its information back to A; C has an independent origin.
samples: B copies A; C counts independently. | B and C both copy A.

stem: Record one people detail and its maker in your topic log.
answer: A supported present-day people detail with its maker: for example, the Council of the Haida Nation describes protecting Haida culture today. Accept a relevant detail from the binational Indigenous organization, naming that maker and its own stated scope.
steps: Accurate detail; named maker; people described in the present. Do not require a universal-language conclusion.
samples: The Haida Nation's council describes its work today. | All Indigenous peoples are one people.

stem: Fill the government table, one office and function per row.
answer: Canada: parliamentary democracy within a constitutional monarchy; prime minister leads government; Parliament makes laws; courts interpret laws and resolve disputes. Mexico and United States: federal presidential republics; presidents lead executive branches; Congress makes laws; courts interpret/apply laws or administer justice. Source for each country. No comparison sentences required.
steps: Each country has its correct offices, functions and source; record each component separately.
samples: Canada: Parliament makes laws. | The prime minister is a president.

stem: Record a city, land feature, resource, and landmark with their sources.
answer: Canada: Ottawa in Ontario, Canada; Rideau Canal, a built waterway and historic landmark; wood, a natural resource. Mexico: Mexico City, Mexico; Chapultepec hill, natural land; castle museum, historic landmark; water, a natural resource. Cite the selected locator and relevant source cards. samples: Ottawa; canal waterway; cite canal page. | This map proves warmth.

stem: Explain one resource-to-industry link from your country notes.

steps: Names resource and work; explains how the material or water supports that work; cites source. No resident-job limit required in this practice response.
samples: Water used for agriculture supports growing crops. | Everyone works in one industry.

stem: Draft your individual country report from the six topic headings.
answer: Practice six-topic draft with map, four kinds and analyzed relationship. Feedback only; score revision on 29.

samples: Topic-ordered report links findings to sources. | A list without sources.

stem: Present a finding with its source.
answer: Practice finding; thirty 45-second teacher-heard slots in 23 minutes. Feedback before 29.
steps: Performs named component using supplied evidence; written feedback; content separate from grammar.
samples: My card explains courts' job. | I like it.

stem: Suggest an order change on your partner's report.
answer: Criterion-linked order improvement; no accuracy rehearsal. Retain as evidence for s02-E11; no separate practice score.
steps: Performs named component using supplied evidence; written feedback; content separate from grammar.
samples: Put the city heading before its details. | I like it.

stem: Label the input and buyer on the made-up printing chain.
answer: Paper input; notebook customers buyers. Component labels only.
steps: Performs named component using supplied evidence; written feedback; content separate from grammar.
samples: Paper: input. Customers: buyers. | Paper is the buyer.

stem: Mark the origin of each teaching-map arrow.
answer: Wheat: Canada; vegetables: Mexico. Origins only.
steps: Performs named component using supplied evidence; written feedback; content separate from grammar.

stem: Annotate one group's changed purchase on the printing cards.

steps: Names each specific group and its own changed purchase, price or order. Does not infer every resident has the same result.
samples: A printing shop gets another order. | All change alike.

stem: Correct one supplied causal link in the factory-or-farm diagram.

samples: The buyer switches supplier, so this farm loses its orders. | The national goods total proves this farm sells less.

stem: Sort your notes under the given claim headings.

steps: Performs named component using supplied evidence; written feedback; content separate from grammar.
samples: The foreign affairs article names wheat crossing to Mexico, under supply connections. | The title proves everyone gains.

stem: Use the supplied paragraph and established notes. Replace its weak evidence link.

stem: Match the already labeled practice claims to their metadata.
answer: Match the reviewed notice's maker caretakers' office, date 2010, audience caretakers, purpose equipment preparation and format posted notice to their fields.
steps: Performs named component using supplied evidence; written feedback; content separate from grammar.
samples: Maker: caretakers' office; date: 2010; audience: caretakers. | Audience: 2010.

stem: Write a claim supported by one detail from the bus diagram.
